'''''Caroxylon vermiculatum''''', commonly known as '''Mediterranean saltwort''', is a perennial plant in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Amaranthaceae]]. It has many [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonyms]], including '''''Salsola vermiculata''''' and '''''Nitrosalsola vermiculata'''''.<ref name=POWO_77089168-1/> It is native to arid and semi-arid regions of the [[Middle East]], North Africa and southern Europe where it is used as a fodder plant for [[livestock]].

==Description==
''Caroxylon vermiculatum'' is a small, greyish, much-branched shrub ranging in height from {{convert|25|to|100|cm|-1|abbr=on}}. The branches themselves branch repeatedly and are wiry and woody at the base. The leaves are tiny and scale-like, clasping the stem and covered with minute hairs. The inflorescence is a leafy spike with solitary flowers in the axils of the leaves. The flowers have persistent, pinkish, winged sepals and no petals and are about {{convert|10|mm|in|1|abbr=on}} in diameter.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.plantwise.org/KnowledgeBank/Datasheet.aspx?dsid=48244 |title=Mediterranean saltwort (''Salsola vermiculata'')
|work=Plantwise Knowledge Bank |accessdate=29 December 2015}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
The species was first described, as ''Salsola vermiculata'', in 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in ''[[Species Plantarum]]''. Phylogenetic research led to the re-circumscription of the genus ''[[Salsola]]'', and in 2007, the species was transferred to ''Caroxylon vermiculatum'' <small>(L.) Akhani & Roalson</small>.<ref name="Akhani">Akhani, H., et al. (2007). Diversification of the Old World Salsoleae ''s.l.'' (Chenopodiaceae): Molecular phylogenetic analysis of nuclear and chloroplast data sets and a revised classification.] ''International Journal of Plant Sciences'', 168(6), 931–56.</ref> In 2015, it was transferred to ''Nitrosalsola vermiculata'' <small>(L.) Theodorova</small>.<ref>Theodorova (Feodorova), T.A. 2015. New nomenclatural combinations in ''Nitrosalsola'' (Chenopodiaceae). Ukrayins'kyi Botanicnyi Zhurnal 72(5): 442–445. doi:10.15407/ukrbotj72.05.442, p.444.</ref> {{As of|2022|April}}, the accepted name in [[Plants of the World Online]] is ''Caroxylon vermiculatum''.<ref name=POWO_77089168-1/>

==Distribution and habitat==
This plant is native to Syria, Lebanon, Israel, Jordan and Saudi Arabia, as well as Egypt and Morocco. It is also native to southern Europe, including Italy, Spain and Portugal.  Its natural habitat is semi-arid and arid grassland, and it has been introduced to Pakistan and to California to provide forage in arid locations. In California it has become a [[weed]] and is regarded as an [[invasive species]].<ref name=CABI>{{cite web |url=http://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/48244 |title=''Salsola vermiculata'' (Mediterranean saltwort) |date=15 May 2008 |work=Invasive Species Compendium |publisher=CABI |accessdate=30 December 2015}}</ref>

==Ecology==
''Caroxylon vermiculatum'' is part of the [[climax community]] in the [[Syrian steppe]] where it grows alongside ''[[Artemisia herba-alba]]'', ''[[Atriplex leucoclada]]'' and ''[[Stipa barbata]]''.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Suttie, J.M.|author2=Reynolds, Stephen G.|author3=Batello, Caterina |title=Grasslands of the World |url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_BBA_HxFizNgC |year=2005 |publisher=FAO |isbn=978-92-5-105337-9 |page=[https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_BBA_HxFizNgC/page/n473 453]}}</ref> It also grows on the Jordanian steppe along with ''Artemisia herba-alba'' and ''[[Achillea fragrantissima]]'', but all three of these useful fodder species are becoming increasingly rare because of [[overgrazing]].<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Al-Tabini1, Raed |author2=Al-Khalidi, Khalid |author3=Al-Shudiefat, Mustafa |year=2012 |title=Livestock, medicinal plants and rangeland viability in Jordan's Badia: through the lens of traditional and local knowledge |journal=Pastoralism: Research, Policy and Practice |volume=2 |issue=4 |page=4 |doi=10.1186/2041-7136-2-4 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2012Pasto...2....4A }}</ref> Exclusion of livestock from an area produces a large increase in the biomass of these species.{{Citation needed|date=December 2019|reason=removed citation to predatory publisher content}}  It has a high protein content and is of high value as a forage crop in arid areas. It is planted in the Middle East for grazing by cattle, sheep, goats and camels.<ref name=CABI/>

Natural regeneration occurs in both spring and autumn, but plants germinating in autumn are more drought tolerant and more likely to become established.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Al-Satari, Yahya |author2=Al Omary, Ayed |author3=Mhawish, Yasser Mahmood |author4=Al-Kabneh, Awad Khalaf |author5=Khrist, Zein Suleiman |author6=Al-Swa’ar, Malik Samih |year=2014 |title=Abundance of natural Regeneration of ''Atriplex halimus'' and ''Salsola vermiculata'' and productivity in the Jordanian Badia |journal=Journal (Academy of Hospital Administration (India)) |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=9–18 |issn=0970-9452 }}</ref> [[Rainwater harvesting]], in the form of contouring furrows that prevent run-off, increases the successful establishment and growth of ''C. vermiculatum''. Planting this and other native species, such as ''[[Atriplex halimus]]'', shows high potential for the improvement of the Badia rangelands in Syria. Prolonged drought sometimes caused the plants to shed their leaves.{{Citation needed|date=December 2019|reason=removed citation to predatory publisher content}}

In California, ''C. vermiculatum'' has been shown to be an [[Host (biology)|alternate host]] for the [[plant virus]]es that cause [[curly top]], a disease of [[sugar beet]], [[tomato]]es and [[Cucurbitaceae|cucurbits]].<ref name=CABI/>
